## Section 4 – Conrad Waddington and Systems Biology Foundations ([00:07:27]).

Next one, please. First of all, this guy has got to be one of the most cited biologists of all time. That's Conrad Waddington, a British developmental biologist, etc., etc., etc., as you see, and also a philosopher. And he is credited with laying the foundations for systems biology, important in the epigenetic field and evolutionary developmental biology. So here's a quote from him. I have two of them. To suppose the evolution of the wonderfully adapted biological mechanisms has depended only on a haphazard set of variations, each produced by blind chance, is like suggesting that if we went out on throwing bricks together into heaps, we should eventually be able to choose ourselves the most desirable house.

And the next one, also a Waddington quote, and I've been aware of this quote for a long time, but it's so important, I think, to Bowen theory. It is the understanding of the nature of the networks of interaction, which are involved in the process in which a collection of cells becomes organized into an organ with a unitary character. That still remains the central question when addressing living beings. How do these networks of interaction, what are they and how do they do this?

## Section 5 – Robert Weinberg on Cancer Complexity and Paradigm Shift ([00:09:11]).

Next one, please. As Robert Weinberg, I put his picture on because he was the discoverer of the first oncogene, the so-called genes that were associated heavily with the development of cancer that were assumed to be the driving force behind cancer. So this is a shift from focusing on the cancer cells and trying to kill them versus focusing on the larger network of tissue in which it exists and how that's become permissive to the development of a cancer. Two quotes from him, the first one, as Robert Weinberg lamented in 2014, we seem to have again misjudged the complexity of the problem. With cancer incidences on the rise and very limited progress in finding cancer cures over the past four decades. And perhaps we have also misjudged how to address complexity.

Next one, a revised theory of cancer may be needed to shift the current paradigm, a theory that incorporates the immaterial processes of evolutionary disfunction that create niches in which the cancer state arises. I don't know how well I can interpret that. I won't try to. It just, it is what it is and a big shift for him since he has been one of the reductionistic researchers hell bent for finding the answer to stopping cancer through studying cancer cells alone.

And this is now we'll go into the extension.

And of course, Darwin introduced the idea of natural selection, didn't know exactly how it worked. And then when the discovery of genes came along, that that was the modern synthesis, putting those two ideas together.

Next slide. So the EES emphasizes the role of the of developmental processes that occur in an organism's lifetime and how dysfunctions in evolutionary programs cannot be reduced to dysfunction in genes. And that's anything but reductionistic. That's standing back and expansive mode.

## Section 14 – Emergence and Integral Interactive Networks ([00:21:12]).

Next one, please. In any systems approach, molecules and phenotypes, phenotype is what a cell can develop, a kidney cell is one type of phenotype, even has the same genes as a liver cell, which is another phenotype, are viewed as integral emergent entities of an interactive network. Emergence is a key word in systems thinking, looking at systems and phenomena emerge out of these complex interactions going on. Really the genes themselves do not control that. They're a kind of blueprint, I guess, I'm not sure the best word there, but they're not in charge.

And maybe to some extent, that's the difficulty that people sometimes have with bone theories, trying to think about all the moving parts. ## Section 30 – Q&A: Kathy on Patient Agency and Medical Decision-Making ([01:25:09]).

I had a couple of thoughts. Years ago, I had the good fortune to be with a good friend as her ride home after getting a biopsy and initial cell slide presentation when the surgeon came into the room and asked her if she wanted me to stay or not. She said yes. And I got to hear him present to her what he had found, which was cancer. And then his initial recommendations for how to proceed. And he said, there are two courses that I recommend. One is pick the best doctor you can find and do what they recommend. And the second is to become your own doctor and decide what you're going to do based on all your research. He said, don't mix up those two things. Those people die. And within the next year.
